options.metric: Police-reported crashes per observed clock hour
options.denominator: Observed clock hours in each window across 5,094 calendar dates (71,316 day-window hours; 50,940 night-window hours)
options.grouping: Day (6 a.m.–7:59 p.m.) vs night (8 p.m.–5:59 a.m.)
options.reason: This compares reported crash burden per unit of clock time while accounting for the unequal lengths of the day and night windows.
options.answer: The data show 24.0 reported crashes per observed clock hour in the 6 a.m.–7:59 p.m. window versus 11.0 at night, but not greater per-trip risk.
options.interpretation: This framing compares reported crash volume across the two time windows after accounting for their unequal lengths and the 5,094-day observation span. It shows about 2.2 times more crashes per clock hour in the day window, making it a defensible measure of reported crash burden over time. It leaves unanswered whether nighttime travel is riskier per trip or per vehicle-mile because traffic exposure is unavailable.

options.metric: Percentage of crashes involving at least one injured or killed person
options.denominator: All police-reported crashes in each time window
options.grouping: Day (6 a.m.–7:59 p.m.) vs night (8 p.m.–5:59 a.m.)
options.reason: This measures how often a recorded crash results in human harm and compares severity without relying on raw crash totals.
options.answer: 28.5% of nighttime crashes involved at least one injured or killed person, compared with 23.5% of daytime crashes.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether a reported crash is more likely to involve human harm at night: the share is 28.5% at night and 23.5% during the day. It is defensible because it compares crash outcomes conditional on a recorded crash rather than comparing raw totals across windows of different lengths. It leaves unanswered whether an individual trip is more likely to end in a crash at night, since traffic exposure is not in this dataset.
